Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 How to Play 3 Action Phase 3.1 Travel 3.2 Perform action 3.3 Promote a Specialist 3.4 Trade with the locals 3.5 Build a Structure 3.6 Summon an Ally 3.7 Purchase an Action Card 4 End Phase 4.1 Refill hand 4.2 Castle income 4.3 Ally income 4.4 Reorganization 5 End of the Game 6 House Action Cards Overview As Frederick II's vassal, you will perform tasks such as summoning Allies from around the Mediterranean, building Structures in your castle, and promoting Specialists to improve your kingdom. Certain actions will trigger Edicts that affect Frederick's Palace, and determine the rewards players may receive from their Allies. You may improve your chances by upgrading your castles: Towers house additional Allies, Walls store more Resources, and Keeps aid in managing Action Cards. The players will take turns during the game, going clockwise, until one of the game end conditions is met. How to Play Stupor Mundi is played over a variable number of rounds, each of which is divided into two phases: the Action Phase , played in clockwise turn order Travel Perform action the End Phase , performed simultaneously by all players. Refill hand Castle income Ally income Reorganization Action Phase Travel [TRAVEL] At the start of your turn, you may choose to travel. To travel, move your Ship 1-4 spaces clockwise around the Voyage Board, paying 1 Augustalis for each space moved. You may then perform your turn action as normal. Perform action [PLAYCARD] Action Cards may be played face-up or face-down in any Action Card slot of your choice, and any sequence – you are not required to play the Action Cards from left to right. Note: At the beginning of the game, the rightmost slot of each player’s Action Board is locked and may not be used. Building a specific Keep during the game will allow you to remove the tile blocking that card slot. Playing a card face-up will allow you to perform the action displayed on that card. Playing a card face-down will allow you to perform one of the board actions pointed to by the soldiers’ spears on the back of that card. Once you have resolved the actions associated with your played card, the next player will take their turn. That player must choose to travel (or not), and then play an Action Card. If a player cannot or does not want to play an Action Card, they must pass their turn. A player who has passed may not travel nor play any more Action Cards in that round. This process continues until all players have passed. Promote a Specialist [PROMOTE] This action allows you to move one of your Specialists one space along one of the three paths on the Workplace Area. Specialists move from one Workplace space to the next, following the arrows. the Workplace Area is divided into 3 areas. From left to right, these are the Countryside (blue), Village (yellow), and City (green) areas. Each area uses different Workplace tiles. Each Countryside and Village tile has two Workplaces, which provide special abilities if you have at least one Specialist in that Workplace. City Workplaces offer one-time bonuses. When your Specialist reaches a City Workplace, take a City bonus tile of your choice (if available), receive the indicated bonus. If a Specialist’s move would cause it to pass over an arrow accompanied by a Grain symbol [GRAIN], you must pay a Grain to the supply before your Specialist may move forward. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Not impressed. A swell of little/fiddly mechanics that don't dovetail particularly well. Ship movement, this-or-that action selection, castle building, specialist tracks, edicts—everything is fine and innocuous on its own, but the combination is messy and inelegant. There’s zero flow. Nothing progresses naturally or intuitively. The decisions aren’t adequately weighty or rewarding.

[Rating: 1/10] Super unbalanced. The back position can't operate at all. I've been behind for 15 rounds in a row. All the good resource cards have been taken away by the front position. Only garbage cards are left. What a garbage game. Have you tested it?

[Rating: 2/10] Way too long, pointless deck building, card & iconography madness (seven whole pages to explain them!). Very few interesting decisions, slow and boring resource management.  One of the worst euro games I’ve ever played.

[Rating: 4/10] After the first play, the game showed promise and felt like a solid 7/10. However, the interaction with the middle castle mechanic quickly revealed itself to be wonky and unreliable, failing to deliver the strategic depth it suggests. Following several plays both IRL and on BGA, my rating has unfortunately dropped to 4/10 = "Not so good - but could play again." [Rating: 4/10] Initial Impressions: I thought I would like the deckbuilding action system, but not the weird sort of commodity speculation point income system. The latter turned out to be correct. But also it turns out while the concept of the deckbuilding is interesting how everything all fits together feels too restraining. You have build restrictions, you have resource limit restrictions, you have to move around the rondel to get to certain places to acquire certain things, you have limitations on your card slots. Any of those by themselves isn't very complicated and in fact could be quite fun in itself, 

[Rating: 4/10] Stupor Mundi has some interesting mechanics but I'm not sure the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.   There is a ship that may sail to location with different trading opportunities and action cards that may trigger either a card action or a player board action. Those actions are used to collect resources, build a castle for more income, advance along tracks for better abilities or buy more cards for better actions and victory points. There is also a strange tug of war game where you add to or remove from Frederick II:s castle to fulfil your objectives/ruin your opponents' objectives. 

[Rating: 5/10] There are pretty cool things in there (nothing new, though), but the overall game is just no good enough. All the stuff there is doesn't fit together too well. There isn't much interaction as well.  I really liked the abilities you can get from the tracks and built stuff, as you can strategize with them in an interesting way. I didn't mind the slight deck building there is, but the decrees make it chaotic and kinda random. [Rating: 5/10] Some clever ideas but really tedious, slow, and over-long.  Desperately needed an editor.

[Rating: 5/10] The mechanics are good and well intertwined, the design is neat. But even if you optimize and plan, it is frustrating to get the decrees at the wrong time or a constellation with other players that just won't favor you. Feels a bit random and not rewarding sometimes

[Rating: 5/10] Economy is a little modern and opaque. Can take a lot of intermediate steps to arrive to the point of "I trade two goods for the thing". The turns can be quick, or very long with AP and combos. It's nice that the purple player acts as a medium of interaction, but it feels too swingy with you just setting up other players to tug it in directions you didn't intend.
